items.stem: A mapping in which every element of the domain has exactly one image, and no two elements share an image, is called
items.markingKey: Each input has one output and each output comes from only one input.

items.stem: Explain why f(x) = x² − 4x, x ∈ ℝ, is not a one-one function.
items.answer: Different inputs give the same output: f(0) = f(4) = 0, so it is many-one (the graph is symmetrical about x = 2).
items.markingKey: B1 example of two inputs with equal images; B1 hence many-one [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the domain and the range of a function.
items.answer: The domain is the set of input values for which the function is defined; the range is the set of output values that the function actually takes.
items.markingKey: B1 domain = inputs; B1 range = outputs/images [2]

items.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = −x − 8 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 5. Find the range of f.
items.markingKey: M1 evaluates f(1) and f(5); A1 −13 ≤ f(x) ≤ −9

items.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² + 6x + 8 for −6 ≤ x ≤ 2. (a) Explain why f is not one-one. (b) Solve the equation f(x) = 15.
items.answer: (a) The vertex x = −3 lies inside the domain, so e.g. f(−4) = f(−2). (b) x = 1

items.stem: Explain how the horizontal line test shows whether a function is one-one.
items.answer: If every horizontal line meets the graph at most once, no output comes from two inputs, so the function is one-one.
items.markingKey: B1 horizontal line meets graph at most once; B1 links to each image having one input [2]

items.stem: Explain why the range of f(x) = (x − 3)² + 1 for x ≥ 5 is f(x) ≥ 5 and not f(x) ≥ 1.
items.answer: For x ≥ 5 the function is increasing (the vertex x = 3 is outside the domain), so the least value is f(5) = 5.
items.markingKey: B1 vertex not in domain / f increasing for x ≥ 5; B1 least value f(5) = 5 [2]

items.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = x² − 7 for −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Lina says the range is −3 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2 because f(−2) = −3 and f(3) = 2. Explain why Lina is wrong and state the correct range.
items.answer: The vertex x = 0 lies inside the domain, so the least value is f(0) = −7, not an end value. Range −7 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2.
items.markingKey: B1 minimum at vertex (0, −7) inside the domain; B1 −7 ≤ f(x) ≤ 2

items.stem: The composite function fg(x) means
options: f(g(x)): apply g first, then f
g(f(x)): apply f first, then g
items.answer: f(g(x)): apply g first, then f
items.markingKey: In fg the function nearest x, g, acts first.

items.stem: Explain why, in general, fg(x) ≠ gf(x), using f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 1.
items.answer: fg(x) = (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1 while gf(x) = x² + 1; the order of the functions changes the result.
items.markingKey: B1 both composites correct; B1 states they differ so order matters [2]

items.stem: f(x) = √x for x ≥ 0 and g(x) = x − 5 for x ∈ ℝ. Explain why fg does not exist.
items.answer: g can take negative values (e.g. g(0) = −5), which are not in the domain of f, so the range of g is not contained in the domain of f.
items.markingKey: B1 range of g includes negatives; B1 not within domain of f [2]

items.stem: The functions f and g are defined by f(x) = 3x + 2 for x ∈ ℝ and g(x) = x² + 2 for x ≥ 0. (a) Find an expression for gf(x) and state why gf, defined for x ∈ ℝ, does not exist. (b) Find ff(x) and solve ff(x) = 44.
items.answer: (a) gf(x) = (3x + 2)² + 2; f(x) takes negative values, which are outside the domain x ≥ 0 of g. (b) ff(x) = 9x + 8; x = 4
items.markingKey: (a) B1 (3x + 2)² + 2; B1 range of f (ℝ) not within domain of g [2] (b) B1 ff(x) = 9x + 8; B1 x = 4 [2]

items.stem: For the composite function fg to exist, which condition must hold?
options: the range of f lies within the domain of g
the domain of f equals the domain of g
the range of g lies within the domain of f
f and g are both one-one
items.answer: the range of g lies within the domain of f
items.markingKey: Every output of g must be a valid input of f.

items.stem: The functions f and g are defined for x ∈ ℝ by f(x) = −4x + 4 and g(x) = x² − 1. Find fg(−3).
Explain why the domain of fg is the same as the domain of g when fg exists.
items.answer: fg(x) = f(g(x)) starts by applying g, so x must be a valid input of g; if fg exists every g(x) is already in the domain of f.
items.markingKey: B1 g acts first; B1 no further restriction when range g ⊆ domain f [2]

items.stem: The functions f and g are defined by f(x) = x² + 6 for x ∈ ℝ and g(x) = √(x − 3) for x ≥ 3. Determine, with a reason, whether the composite function gf exists.
items.answer: Yes: the range of f is f(x) ≥ 6, which lies within the domain x ≥ 3 of g, so gf exists.
items.markingKey: B1 range of f is f(x) ≥ 6; B1 contained in domain of g so gf exists

items.stem: The functions f and g are defined by f(x) = x² − 5 for x ∈ ℝ and g(x) = √(x + 2) for x ≥ −2. Determine, with a reason, whether the composite function gf exists.
items.answer: No: the range of f is f(x) ≥ −5, which includes values less than −2 (e.g. f(0) = −5), and these are not in the domain of g.
items.markingKey: B1 range of f is f(x) ≥ −5; B1 not contained in x ≥ −2 so gf does not exist

items.stem: Explain why f(x) = x² for x ∈ ℝ has no inverse, and state how the domain could be restricted so that an inverse exists.
items.answer: f is many-one (f(2) = f(−2)), so it cannot be reversed. Restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 makes it one-one.

items.stem: Explain why ff⁻¹(x) = x for every x in the domain of f⁻¹.
items.answer: f⁻¹ maps x to the value whose image under f is x, so applying f afterwards returns x.
items.markingKey: B1 f⁻¹ undoes f; B1 composition gives identity [2]

items.answer: The graphs are reflections of each other in y = x; for an increasing function they can only meet on that mirror line, so solving f(x) = x gives the intersections.

items.stem: Explain the difference between f⁻¹(x) and 1/f(x).
items.answer: f⁻¹ is the inverse function, which undoes f; 1/f(x) is the reciprocal of the value of f. For f(x) = 2x, f⁻¹(x) = x/2 but 1/f(x) = 1/(2x).
items.markingKey: B1 inverse undoes f vs reciprocal; B1 example showing they differ [2]

items.markingKey: B1 reciprocal is not the inverse (e.g. f⁻¹(f(0)) ≠ 0 with this formula); B1 f⁻¹(x) = (x + 6)/4

items.stem: Explain why y = f(x − 3) is a translation of y = f(x) by 3 units in the positive x-direction, not the negative direction.

items.stem: Explain why the order of the transformations matters when y = f(x) is transformed to y = 2f(x) + 3.

items.stem: Priya transforms y = f(x) by first translating by (0, −1) and then stretching parallel to the y-axis with scale factor 7. Priya writes the result as y = 7f(x) − 1. Explain the error and state the correct equation.
items.answer: The stretch acts on the whole translated function: 7(f(x) − 1) = 7f(x) − 7. Priya's equation corresponds to stretching first.
items.markingKey: B1 stretch multiplies the constant too / order matters; B1 y = 7f(x) − 7

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why y = f(x − 3) is a translation of y = f(x) by 3 units in the positive x-direction, not the negative direction. (b) Describe the effect of the transformation y = f(x) → y = f(x/2) on the point (3, 5).
items.answer: (a) The new graph takes at x the value f had at x − 3, i.e. 3 units earlier, so every point moves 3 units to the right. (b) It is a stretch parallel to the x-axis with scale factor 2, so (3, 5) moves to (6, 5).
items.markingKey: (a) B1 value at x equals old value at x − 3; B1 shift right by 3 [2] (b) B1 stretch factor 2 in x-direction; B1 (6, 5) [2]

items.stem: The function g is defined by g(x) = x² + 8x + 9 for x ≥ −7. Determine, with a reason, whether g is one-one.
items.answer: No: the vertex is at x = −4 > −7, so values on either side of x = −4 give equal images, e.g. g(−5) = g(−3) = −6.
items.markingKey: B1 vertex at x = −4 inside domain; B1 example of equal images so not one-one

items.stem: f(x) = x² and g(x) = x − 1. Which expression is fg(x)?
Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the domain of fg is the same as the domain of g when fg exists. (b) f(x) = √x for x ≥ 0 and g(x) = x − 5 for x ∈ ℝ. Explain why fg does not exist.
items.answer: (a) fg(x) = f(g(x)) starts by applying g, so x must be a valid input of g; if fg exists every g(x) is already in the domain of f. (b) g can take negative values (e.g. g(0) = −5), which are not in the domain of f, so the range of g is not contained in the domain of f.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 g acts first; B1 no further restriction when range g ⊆ domain f [2] (b) B1 range of g includes negatives; B1 not within domain of f [2]

items.answer: (a) 4x² + 10 (b) gf(x) = (4x + 2)² + 2; f(x) takes negative values, which are outside the domain x ≥ 0 of g. (c) fg(x) ≥ 10 (d) ff(x) = 16x + 10; x = 1
items.markingKey: (a) B1 fg(x) = 4x² + 10 [1] (b) B1 (4x + 2)² + 2; B1 range of f (ℝ) not within domain of g [2] (c) B1 fg(x) ≥ 10 [1] (d) B1 ff(x) = 16x + 10; B1 x = 1 [2]

items.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = (x − 5)² − 4 for x ≥ 5. Grace finds f⁻¹(x) = 5 − √(x + 4). Explain why this is incorrect and give f⁻¹(x) correctly, stating its domain.
items.answer: The range of f⁻¹ must be the domain of f, x ≥ 5, so the positive root is needed: f⁻¹(x) = 5 + √(x + 4) for x ≥ −4.
items.markingKey: B1 range of f⁻¹ = domain of f, x ≥ 5, so + root; B1 f⁻¹(x) = 5 + √(x + 4), x ≥ −4

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the order of the transformations matters when y = f(x) is transformed to y = 2f(x) + 3. (b) Describe the effect of the transformation y = f(x) → y = f(x/2) on the point (3, 5).
items.answer: (a) Stretching by 2 then translating by 3 gives 2f(x) + 3; translating first then stretching gives 2(f(x) + 3) = 2f(x) + 6, a different curve. (b) It is a stretch parallel to the x-axis with scale factor 2, so (3, 5) moves to (6, 5).
items.markingKey: (a) B1 stretch then translate; B1 other order gives 2f(x) + 6 [2] (b) B1 stretch factor 2 in x-direction; B1 (6, 5) [2]
